Lecture 32

Separation of variables and a finite string

We find the modes of the string with fixed ends and prove a theorem on sine series: mean-square convergence for piecewise continuous functions, pointwise convergence for piecewise C1C^1C1 functions and uniform convergence for continuous piecewise C1C^1C1 functions that vanish at the ends. We then solve the string, share its energy among the modes and interpret a plucked string.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Find the modes and frequencies of a string with fixed ends by separation of variables.
  • Compute sine coefficients and state how the sine series of given data converges.
  • Construct the series solution, check when it is a classical solution, and compute its energy mode by mode.
  • Interpret the series of a plucked string as its d’Alembert solution and bound the truncation error.

Lecture 31 solved the string on the whole line and on a half-line. A guitar string has two fixed ends. In this lecture we describe its motion as a sum of standing waves, the normal modes of the string. The lecture reads in four stages: the modes and the coefficients (Sections 32.1–32.2), the theorem on sine series (Section 32.3), the string solved, with its energy (Sections 32.4–32.6), and a plucked string (Section 32.7).

Throughout the lecture L>0L>0L>0 and c>0c>0c>0, and the string with fixed ends is the problem utt=c2uxx(0<x<L, t>0),u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0(t≥0),u(x,0)=u0(x),ut(x,0)=v0(x)(0≤x≤L).\begin{gathered} u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}\quad(0<x<L,\ t>0),\qquad u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0\quad(t\ge0),\\ u(x,0)=u_0(x),\quad u_t(x,0)=v_0(x)\quad(0\le x\le L). \end{gathered}utt​=c2uxx​(0<x<L, t>0),u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0(t≥0),u(x,0)=u0​(x),ut​(x,0)=v0​(x)(0≤x≤L).​(32.1) It is Lecture 29’s string with f=0f=0f=0 and fixed ends. A number λ∈C\lambda\in\Cλ∈C is an eigenvalue of the fixed-end problem if −y′′=λyon (0,L),y(0)=y(L)=0,-y''=\lambda y\quad\text{on }(0,L),\qquad y(0)=y(L)=0,−y′′=λyon (0,L),y(0)=y(L)=0, has a solution yyy, twice continuously differentiable on [0,L][0,L][0,L] and not identically zero. This raises two questions: which functions are sums of sine series, with which coefficients, and when the series may be differentiated term by term so that its sum solves the equation. Sections 32.2–32.3 answer the first and Sections 32.4–32.5 the second.

32.2 Orthogonality and sine coefficients

We use Lecture 23’s piecewise continuous and piecewise C1C^1C1 functions on [0,L][0,L][0,L], where the partition into pieces is finite. A piecewise continuous function on [0,L][0,L][0,L] is bounded. As in Lecture 25, the inner product and the norm on (0,L)(0,L)(0,L) are ⟨f,g⟩=∫0Lf(x)‾ g(x) ⁣dx,∥f∥=(∫0L∣f(x)∣2 ⁣dx)1/2,\inner fg=\int_0^L\conj{f(x)}\,g(x)\dd x,\qquad \norm f=\Bigl(\int_0^L\abs{f(x)}^2\dd x\Bigr)^{1/2},⟨f,g⟩=∫0L​f(x)​g(x)dx,∥f∥=(∫0L​∣f(x)∣2dx)1/2,(32.9) and two functions that differ only at finitely many points have the same inner products and the same norm. As in Lecture 25, we identify such functions when we use this inner product and norm. Lecture 25’s Cauchy–Schwarz lemma, applied to fff and ggg extended by zero outside [0,L][0,L][0,L], gives ∣⟨f,g⟩∣≤∥f∥∥g∥\abs{\inner fg}\le\norm f\norm g∣⟨f,g⟩∣≤∥f∥∥g∥. Expanding ∥f+g∥2=∥f∥2+2Re⁡⟨f,g⟩+∥g∥2≤(∥f∥+∥g∥)2\norm{f+g}^2=\norm f^2+2\Re\inner fg+\norm g^2\le(\norm f+\norm g)^2∥f+g∥2=∥f∥2+2Re⟨f,g⟩+∥g∥2≤(∥f∥+∥g∥)2 gives the triangle inequality ∥f+g∥≤∥f∥+∥g∥\norm{f+g}\le\norm f+\norm g∥f+g∥≤∥f∥+∥g∥. The sines are orthogonal. For integers m,n≥1m,n\ge1m,n≥1, the identity 2sin⁡(kmx)sin⁡(knx)=cos⁡((km−kn)x)−cos⁡((km+kn)x)2\sin(k_mx)\sin(k_nx)=\cos((k_m-k_n)x)-\cos((k_m+k_n)x)2sin(km​x)sin(kn​x)=cos((km​−kn​)x)−cos((km​+kn​)x) gives ∫0Lsin⁡(kmx)sin⁡(knx) ⁣dx=L2 δmn,∫0Lcos⁡(kmx)cos⁡(knx) ⁣dx=L2 δmn,\int_0^L\sin(k_mx)\sin(k_nx)\dd x=\frac L2\,\delta_{mn},\qquad \int_0^L\cos(k_mx)\cos(k_nx)\dd x=\frac L2\,\delta_{mn},∫0L​sin(km​x)sin(kn​x)dx=2L​δmn​,∫0L​cos(km​x)cos(kn​x)dx=2L​δmn​,(32.10) because ∫0Lcos⁡(kjx) ⁣dx=0\int_0^L\cos(k_jx)\dd x=0∫0L​cos(kj​x)dx=0 for every integer j≠0j\ne0j=0. The second identity follows in the same way from 2cos⁡(kmx)cos⁡(knx)=cos⁡((km−kn)x)+cos⁡((km+kn)x)2\cos(k_mx)\cos(k_nx)=\cos((k_m-k_n)x)+\cos((k_m+k_n)x)2cos(km​x)cos(kn​x)=cos((km​−kn​)x)+cos((km​+kn​)x). So the functions en(x)=2/L sin⁡(knx)e_n(x)=\sqrt{2/L}\,\sin(k_nx)en​(x)=2/L​sin(kn​x), n≥1n\ge1n≥1, are orthonormal, ⟨em,en⟩=δmn\inner{e_m}{e_n}=\delta_{mn}⟨em​,en​⟩=δmn​. Definition 32.3 (Sine and cosine coefficients). For fff piecewise continuous on [0,L][0,L][0,L] the sine coefficients and the cosine coefficients are bn(f)=2L∫0Lf(x)sin⁡(knx) ⁣dx(n≥1),an(f)=2L∫0Lf(x)cos⁡(knx) ⁣dx(n≥0).b_n(f)=\frac2L\int_0^Lf(x)\sin(k_nx)\dd x\quad(n\ge1),\qquad a_n(f)=\frac2L\int_0^Lf(x)\cos(k_nx)\dd x\quad(n\ge0).bn​(f)=L2​∫0L​f(x)sin(kn​x)dx(n≥1),an​(f)=L2​∫0L​f(x)cos(kn​x)dx(n≥0).(32.11) The partial sums of the sine series of fff are SNf(x)=∑n=1Nbn(f)sin⁡(knx)S_Nf(x)=\sum_{n=1}^Nb_n(f)\sin(k_nx)SN​f(x)=∑n=1N​bn​(f)sin(kn​x), N=1,2,…N=1,2,\ldotsN=1,2,….

Thus bn(f)sin⁡(knx)=⟨en,f⟩en(x)b_n(f)\sin(k_nx)=\inner{e_n}fe_n(x)bn​(f)sin(kn​x)=⟨en​,f⟩en​(x), and the coefficients are forced if a series converges uniformly.

Proposition 32.4 (Coefficients of a uniformly convergent series). If the series ∑nγnsin⁡(knx)\sum_n\gamma_n\sin(k_nx)∑n​γn​sin(kn​x) converges uniformly on [0,L][0,L][0,L] to a function fff, then γn=bn(f)\gamma_n=b_n(f)γn​=bn​(f) for every n≥1n\ge1n≥1.

Proof. The terms are continuous, so fff is continuous (GM 30). Multiply the series by sin⁡(kmx)\sin(k_mx)sin(km​x). It still converges uniformly, because ∣sin⁡∣≤1\abs{\sin}\le1∣sin∣≤1. By GM 30’s theorem on the integration of a uniform limit, applied to the real and the imaginary parts, the integral of fsin⁡(kmx)f\sin(k_mx)fsin(km​x) is the sum of the integrals of the terms, and by (32.10) only the term n=mn=mn=m contributes: ∫0Lfsin⁡(kmx) ⁣dx=γmL/2\int_0^Lf\sin(k_mx)\dd x=\gamma_mL/2∫0L​fsin(km​x)dx=γm​L/2. ■

32.3 The theorem on sine series

GM 35 cited the pointwise result for periodic functions. We prove its sine-series form here, with the other convergence statements that the string needs.

Theorem 32.5 (Sine series on (0,L)(0,L)(0,L)). Let fff be piecewise continuous on [0,L][0,L][0,L].

  • Best approximation and Bessel’s inequality. For every NNN and all numbers γ1,…,γN\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_Nγ1​,…,γN​, ∥f−∑n=1Nγnsin⁡(knx)∥2=∥f−SNf∥2+L2∑n=1N∣bn(f)−γn∣2,∥f−SNf∥2=∥f∥2−L2∑n=1N∣bn(f)∣2.\begin{aligned} \norm{f-\sum_{n=1}^N\gamma_n\sin(k_nx)}^2&=\norm{f-S_Nf}^2+\frac L2\sum_{n=1}^N\abs{b_n(f)-\gamma_n}^2,\\ \norm{f-S_Nf}^2&=\norm f^2-\frac L2\sum_{n=1}^N\abs{b_n(f)}^2 . \end{aligned}​f−n=1∑N​γn​sin(kn​x)​2∥f−SN​f∥2​=∥f−SN​f∥2+2L​n=1∑N​∣bn​(f)−γn​∣2,=∥f∥2−2L​n=1∑N​∣bn​(f)∣2.​(32.12) In particular L2∑n=1∞∣bn(f)∣2≤∥f∥2\frac L2\sum_{n=1}^\infty\abs{b_n(f)}^2\le\norm f^22L​∑n=1∞​∣bn​(f)∣2≤∥f∥2. The same holds for the cosine coefficients: L2∑n=1∞∣an(f)∣2≤∥f∥2\frac L2\sum_{n=1}^\infty\abs{a_n(f)}^2\le\norm f^22L​∑n=1∞​∣an​(f)∣2≤∥f∥2.

Parseval’s identity, equivalently the mean-square convergence of every sine series of a piecewise continuous fff, is the completeness of the sines. In particular such an fff with zero sine coefficients is zero off finitely many points. The extension to all square-integrable functions needs the Lebesgue integral (AN 6, the theorem that the sines form an orthonormal basis of L2(0,L)L^2(0,L)L2(0,L)), and we do not need it.

32.4 Decay and termwise differentiation

Decay of the sine coefficients lets us differentiate a series term by term. GM 31 proved termwise differentiation for power series only, so we first prove the version we need.

32.7 A plucked string

A guitar string is plucked by pulling one point aside and releasing it, as in Lecture 31’s triangular pluck. Its initial shape has corners, so Theorem 32.9 does not apply. The series still converges, and it gives Lecture 31’s d’Alembert solution.

So the series of a plucked string is the weaker solution that Lecture 31 defined, not a classical one. Its partial sums are classical solutions with the initial data SNu0S_Nu_0SN​u0​ and SNv0S_Nv_0SN​v0​, and they converge to it uniformly. The termwise second derivatives do not converge in general. For the pluck below kn2bnk_n^2b_nkn2​bn​ does not even tend to zero. For the data of Theorem 32.9 the classical solution is (32.20), with reflections of opposite sign at both ends, and every motion repeats. On the whole line of Lecture 31 a localized pulse travels away and never returns.

Example 32.13 (A string plucked at its midpoint). We expand a plucked string in modes, check its energy and compare the truncation error with that of Example 32.10. Summary

Separating the variables of a string with fixed ends gives the modes, standing waves with the harmonic frequencies ωn=nπc/L\omega_n=n\pi c/Lωn​=nπc/L. Sine series converge in the mean square, pointwise and uniformly under increasing hypotheses.

  • Modes: eigenvalues kn2k_n^2kn2​, kn=nπ/Lk_n=n\pi/Lkn​=nπ/L, eigenfunctions sin⁡(knx)\sin(k_nx)sin(kn​x); the motion has the period 2L/c2L/c2L/c.

  • Coefficients: bn(f)=2L∫0Lfsin⁡(knx) ⁣dxb_n(f)=\frac2L\int_0^Lf\sin(k_nx)\dd xbn​(f)=L2​∫0L​fsin(kn​x)dx, forced for a uniformly convergent sine series.

  • Sine series on (0,L)(0,L)(0,L): ∥f−SNf∥→0\norm{f-S_Nf}\to0∥f−SN​f∥→0 and Parseval for piecewise continuous fff; the half-sum on (0,L)(0,L)(0,L) for piecewise C1C^1C1 fff; uniform convergence for continuous piecewise C1C^1C1 fff with f(0)=f(L)=0f(0)=f(L)=0f(0)=f(L)=0.

  • Decay: smoothness and vanishing even derivatives at the ends give ∑nm−1∣bn(f)∣<∞\sum n^{m-1}\abs{b_n(f)}<\infty∑nm−1∣bn​(f)∣<∞.

  • String: for u0∈C2u_0\in C^2u0​∈C2 with u0′′u_0''u0′′​ piecewise C1C^1C1 and v0∈C1v_0\in C^1v0​∈C1 with v0′v_0'v0′​ piecewise C1C^1C1, under (32.17) the series (32.16) is the unique classical solution in Lecture 31’s class.

  • Energy: E=∑nρL4(ωn2bn(u0)2+bn(v0)2)E=\sum_n\frac{\rho L}4\bigl(\omega_n^2b_n(u_0)^2+b_n(v_0)^2\bigr)E=∑n​4ρL​(ωn2​bn​(u0​)2+bn​(v0​)2), each term constant.

  • Pluck: the series converges uniformly to the d’Alembert solution of the odd 2L2L2L-periodic extensions; its coefficients decay like n−2n^{-2}n−2.

Lecture 33 solves Laplace’s equation on a rectangle with the same sine series.

References

Preparation: Lecture 7 (constant coefficients), Lecture 14 (normal modes), Lecture 23 (piecewise C1C^1C1 functions, the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma), Lecture 25 (inner product, Cauchy–Schwarz), Lecture 29 (the string, superposition), Lecture 31 (d’Alembert’s formula and solution, energy, uniqueness, the fixed end); GM 9, 12, 25, 26, 29, 30, 31, 35; LA 7–8 (orthonormal bases, as an analogy).
